candidates.title: U.K. Launches Dedicated Squadron to Protect Space Assets
candidates.raw_excerpt: The U.K. Government has made a major new space defense initiative by launching its first ever dedicated squadron to protect its satellites. The No. 3 Space Effects Squadron (SES) will be charged with disrupting, degrading and denying hostile activity to defend U.K. space interests and gain operational advantage for the integrated force. The U.K’s Chief of the Air Staff, Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth announced the formation of this squadron at the U.K. Space Power event in London, Sept. 23. The squadron will be staffed by specialist personnel from across defense and will support offensive and defensive space operations, safeguarding critical space services. The formation of No. 3 Space Effects Squadron aims to contribute to the U.K’s developing capabilities for space warfare, including electronic warfare and countermeasures against anti-satellite weapons. The squadron will protect the critical satellites that guide British ships, connect mobile phones and warn of missile attacks. The U.K. already has No. 1 Space Ops Squadron working as part of the NSPOC and No. 2 Space Warning Squadron delivering operational activity from its RAF Fylingdales. The new No. 3 Space Effects Squadron will aim to deliver precise, integrated effects to safeguard the U.K’s national interests in space. “We are planning more. Numbers 4, 5 and 6 Squadrons, including a Space Tactics and Training Squadron, and squadrons which will deliver the deep space advanced radar capability. We will never escalate military activity in space, but we must respond responsibly to a rapidly changing environment in which threats to our critical space systems are growing every single day,” Smyth said. candidates.raw_excerpt:
South China's Hainan Province is stepping up efforts to build a low-carbon economy, with cleaner energy, greener transportation and a more integrated energy system forming key parts of the transition.

The latest progress came on Wednesday, when the country's first island-loop natural gas pipeline network, the Hainan natural gas network, surpassed 35 billion cubic meters in cumulative gas transmission, according to PipeChina.

The 899-kilometer network has 14 processing stations and 42 valve chambers, passing through 14 cities and counties and serving more than 10 million people. It mainly supplies gas to power plants, industrial users and urban gas customers.

The natural gas transported through the network has replaced an estimated 46.6 million tonnes of coal, reducing dust emissions by more than 25.4 million tonnes and carbon dioxide emissions by more than 51.2 million tonnes, according to PipeChina.

But Hainan's low-carbon transition goes beyond its energy supply.
